title: Calculiva home improvement constants register
rights: CC BY 4.0 covers Calculiva's own contribution only: the compilation, its structure, the statuses, the scopes and the notes. Third-party values (published charts, list prices, product dimensions, tool outputs) are attributed to their sources and dated; no right over them is granted or claimed. Third-party text is not reproduced: each record names the page it was read on, and the excerpts read stay in Calculiva's working files. Calculiva is not affiliated with any company named.

records.label: Epoxy floor coverage: physical basis and observed estimator rules
records.scope: The physical basis is exact and product-independent: one US gallon is 231 cubic inches, one mil is 0.001 inch, so one gallon spread at one mil dry film with 100 percent volume solids covers 231,000 square inches, 1,604.17 square feet. Vendor coverage rates, kit sizes and mix ratios below belong to their publishers on the day tested; they illustrate how public estimators multiply and are never Calculiva defaults. Every thickness, solids figure, loss allowance, kit size, ratio and broadcast rate preloaded in the calculator is a hypothetical exercise to be replaced by the product's technical data sheet.
records.source_name: NIST Handbook 44 Appendix C (gallon = 231 cubic inches) and live executions of ranking epoxy calculators, 10 September 2026
records.values_withheld: Values not redistributed: the publisher's terms do not allow republication. Read them at the source or on the Calculiva page that cites them.

records.label: Loose-fill playground surfacing: minimum depths by equipment height, compression of the initial fill, and how far the surfacing extends

records.scope: Wood mulch or wood chips used as protective surfacing under home play equipment in the United States. The home handbook is the reference; the public handbook is quoted for the 25 percent compression rule and its table. Equipment taller than 8 feet, rubber mulch, sand, pea gravel and unitary mats are outside what the calculator models.

loose_fill.low_equipment_initial_fill_note: The home handbook gives no first fill for the 6-inch case; Calculiva derives 8 inches from the public handbook's 'at least 25%' compression (6 / 0.75).

table_2_minimum_compressed_depths.note: does not compress in the same manner as other loose-fill materials

records.label: Laying sod: brick pattern, cut edges, topsoil and compost under new sod, first watering, as published by four extension services
records.source_name: Penn State Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension; UF/IFAS Extension (LH013, LH010); NC State Extension
records.scope: Solid sod laid by hand on a home lawn in the United States. Each figure belongs to the publisher named and was read on the verification date; Calculiva keeps on file the verbatim excerpts read on 2026-09-25 and does not republish them. No figure is a standard. The four publishers agree on the staggered (brick) pattern; they differ on how much organic matter to work in.

publishers.title: How to select and install sod
Establishing Your Florida Lawn (LH013)
publishers.offcut_reuse: fill cracks with cut up pieces of sod

publishers.title: Carolina Lawns
publishers.organic_when: if planting in heavy clay or very sandy soils

publishers.title: Extension Gardener Handbook, chapter 9: Lawns
publishers.note: Carolina Lawns, from the same publisher, gives about April until July 1 for warm-season sod.

ncsu_organic_as_layer_in.rule: 1 cu yd = 46,656 cu in spread over 1,000 sq ft = 144,000 sq in → 0.324 in; 2 cu yd → 0.648 in
ncsu_organic_as_layer_in.note: NC State's rate, spread as a layer, is about a third to two thirds of an inch; Penn State's layer is 1 to 2 inches.

records.label: Plugging a lawn from solid sod: spacing by species and square feet of sod per 1,000 square feet, UF/IFAS Table 3
records.source_name: UF/IFAS Extension, Establishing Your Florida Lawn (LH013), Table 3; NC State Extension, Carolina Lawns
records.scope: Warm-season grasses planted as 2-inch plugs cut from solid sod, on a square grid. The table is UF/IFAS's, for Florida; the spacing ranges quoted from NC State are for North Carolina. Sprigs are recorded but not modeled.
records.table3_note: The numbers in the column refer to the sq ft of solid sod from which either 2-inch plugs or sprigs can be obtained.

derived.grid_arithmetic: Plugs on a square grid at spacing s cover one plug per s² of lawn: 1,000 sq ft takes 1,000 plugs at 12 in and 4,000 at 6 in. At 324 two-inch plugs per sq yd, that is 27.8 and 111.1 sq ft of sod, just under or at the low end of the Table 3 ranges (30-50 and 100-150).
